front.title: New Canonical Cache Representation (CCR) States for use with Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)

abstract.t: Canonical Cache Representation (CCR) is a Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) encoded data interchange format which can be used to represent various aspects of the state of a validated Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) cache at a particular point in time. CCR is a compact and versatile data format, well-suited for a variety of applications such as audit trails, analytics pipelines, and validated payload dissemination. This document specifies new CCR states and updates RFC-To-Be .

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) operators often wish to analyze Certification Authority (CA) and Relying Party (RP) behaviors by inspecting validation outcomes. To this end, Canonical Cache Representation (CCR) () was developed to capture and archive RPKI validation states in a standardized data representation. CCR is intentionally deterministic and byte-for-byte reproducible across implementations.

CCR offers a compact and versatile format well-suited for applications such as audit trails, analytics pipelines, and validated payload dissemination. A validated cache contains all RPKI objects that the RP has verified to be valid according to the rules for validation (see , , and ). CCR is a data interchange format using Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) which can be used to represent various aspects of the state of a validated cache at a particular point in time in a reproducible manner. Given identical inputs, compliant implementations produce identical CCR encodings.
This document extends the CCR existing data format and provides test vectors for the new state definitions. This document updates RFC-To-Be .

section.name: The Canonical Cache Representation (CCR) Content Type
section.t: The content of a CCR file is an instance of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) ContentInfo.
The contentType for a CCR is defined as id-ct-rpkiCanonicalCacheRepresentation, with Object Identifier (OID) 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.54.
The content field contains an instance of RpkiCanonicalCacheRepresentation, defined in .

section.name: State aspect fields
section.t: Each CCR MUST contain one or more fields representing particular aspects of the cache's state.
Implementers should note the ellipsis extension marker in the RpkiCanonicalCacheRepresentation ASN.1 notation and anticipate future changes as new signed object types are standardized.

Each state aspect generally consists of a sequence of details extracted from RPKI Objects of a specific type, along with a digest computed by hashing the aforementioned DER-encoded sequence, and optionally including some metadata.
See for the specification of CCR states not covered by this specification.

section.name: TrustStoreState
section.t: An instance of TrustStoreState contains the set of valid Trust Anchor (TA) CA resource certificates used by the RP when producing the CCR.
The tscerts field contains a sequence of Certificate instances sorted in ascending order by interpreting the certificate's SubjectKeyIdentifier value as an unsigned 160-bit integer.
The hash field contains a message digest computed using the tscerts value (encoded in DER format) as input message.

section.title: Example CCR
section.t: This section provides a Base64-encoded example CCR object.

This test vector demonstrates various features of the CCR format, for example, the tree-like structure following from TrustAnchorState and ManifestState, multiple authorizations for the same prefix in a ROAPayloadState, an ASPAPayloadState with AS 0 as provider.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on a proposal described in RFC 7942. The description of implementations in this section is intended to assist the IETF in its decision processes in progressing drafts to RFCs. Please note that the listing of any individual implementation here does not imply endorsement by the IETF. Furthermore, no effort has been spent to verify the information presented here that was supplied by IETF contributors. This is not intended as, and must not be construed to be, a catalog of available implementations or their features. Readers are advised to note that other implementations may exist.

According to RFC 7942, "this will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature. It is up to the individual working groups to use this information as they see fit".
